\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Training-free LLM information extraction---prompting a large language model with a target schema and asking it to extract structured information without any task-specific fine-tuning---enables rapid deployment across new domains and ontologies. This zero-shot paradigm eliminates the need for labeled data, making it attractive for applications where annotation is expensive or schemas evolve frequently \cite{llm4ie-survey-2024}. Yet the paradigm carries a critical limitation: performance degrades sharply as the number of candidate types in the prompt schema grows. On named entity recognition, recall drops from 0.72 with a single candidate type to 0.42 with 64 types, a 42\% relative decline. On relation extraction, accuracy falls from 85.7\% with one relation to 50.4\% with 80 relations---near halving. This degradation is not academic: real-world ontologies routinely define 50--200+ types, placing them squarely in the regime where training-free extraction becomes unreliable.

What causes this schema-induced degradation? Prior work has proposed decomposition strategies that implicitly assume different answers. \citet{uniner-2024} extract each type independently, assuming types can be treated as separable. \citet{llm-pee-2025} partition large event schemas by type embedding similarity before extraction, assuming that semantic overlap between co-presented types drives errors. \citet{parse-2025} rewrite and optimize schema definitions, assuming that description quality is the bottleneck. Each approach improves extraction under certain conditions, but none isolates \emph{why} schemas degrade performance in the first place. The closest work, LLM-PEE \cite{llm-pee-2025}, reduces both the number of co-presented types and their inter-type similarity simultaneously, making it impossible to determine which factor---or what combination---accounts for the observed gains. More broadly, all prior approaches conflate two distinct mechanisms that could independently degrade extraction: having more types to discriminate among (count) and having semantically similar types to confuse (confusability). Without disentangling these factors, decomposition strategies cannot be principled: they optimize a black-box objective without understanding its components.

We ask three questions. \textbf{RQ1}: Does type confusability independently predict extraction degradation beyond the effect of type count? \textbf{RQ2}: Through what mechanisms do count and confusability each degrade performance? \textbf{RQ3}: Can confusability-aware schema decomposition improve extraction quality?

To answer these questions, we conduct the first controlled empirical study that isolates type confusability from type count across three IE tasks: named entity recognition (NER), relation extraction (RE), and event detection (ED). We introduce the \emph{Schema Confusability Score} (SCS), which quantifies pairwise semantic overlap between types using embedding cosine similarity, and its batch-level aggregation, the \emph{Batch Confusability Score} (BCS). We design two complementary experimental paradigms: \emph{count curves} that vary schema size while randomizing confusability, and \emph{BCS-controlled experiments} that fix schema size while varying confusability. We evaluate on three datasets spanning diverse schema structures: Few-NERD \cite{fewnerd-2021} (66 entity types across 8 domains), FewRel \cite{fewrel-2018} (80 relation types), and MAVEN \cite{maven-2020} (168 event types from a single ontology). All experiments use Qwen3-32B in a zero-shot prompting setup with bootstrap confidence intervals.

Our experiments yield five findings: (1)~schema-induced degradation operates through two channels---count-driven recall decline (up to $-$30\,pp) and confusability-driven type confusion---that are separable in RE; in NER, confusability additionally impairs entity detection; (2)~pairwise SCS predicts type confusion across tasks ($r = 0.112$--$0.129$), modest in magnitude but the first factor empirically isolated in controlled zero-shot IE; (3)~confusability effects are robust across schema sizes, with BCS--accuracy slopes consistent between 16-type and 80-type pools (permutation $p = 0.60$); (4)~per-type confusability aggregation is confounded by centrality on homogeneous schemas; and (5)~confusability-aware decomposition fails due to merge amplification (best F1 = 0.32 vs.\ single-pass 0.45), a structural challenge for union-based merge pipelines.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=2pt]
    \item \textbf{Multi-channel degradation pattern.} We identify two empirical degradation channels---count and confusability---across NER, RE, and ED, revealing task-dependent channel behavior.
    \item \textbf{Pairwise confusability as a statistically significant but modest predictor.} We demonstrate that pairwise SCS predicts type confusion across tasks and embedding models, while identifying a centrality confound that invalidates per-type aggregation on homogeneous schemas.
    \item \textbf{Cross-task controlled experiments.} We present BCS-controlled experiments with bootstrap confidence intervals on three datasets, establishing that the BCS--accuracy relationship is consistent across schema sizes (slope permutation $p = 0.60$) and that larger type pools produce wider absolute gaps through expanded BCS ranges.
    \item \textbf{Informative negative result.} Our SDGD experiments identify merge amplification as a structural challenge for union-based merge approaches, with direct implications for the design of schema decomposition methods.
\end{enumerate}

Spearman rank correlations corroborate these findings. Across all type pairs, Qwen3 yields $\rho = 0.168$ ($p = 7.3 \times 10^{-14}$) and MiniLM yields $\rho = 0.144$ ($p = 1.7 \times 10^{-10}$). Restricting to pairs with nonzero confusion strengthens the association: $\rho = 0.272$ for Qwen3 and $\rho = 0.306$ for MiniLM. However, this increase warrants caution: conditioning on nonzero confusion selects for the dependent variable, which can inflate correlations. We report both estimates for transparency; the all-pairs correlations ($r = 0.112\text{--}0.129$) provide the unbiased baseline, while the nonzero-subset values ($\rho = 0.27\text{--}0.31$) characterize the signal among types the model actually confuses.

lines: Spearman rank correlations corroborate these findings. Across all type pairs, Qwen3 yields $\rho = 0.168$ ($p = 7.3 \times 10^{-14}$) and MiniLM yields $\rho = 0.144$ ($p = 1.7 \times 10^{-10}$). Restricting to pairs with nonzero confusion strengthens the association: $\rho = 0.272$ for Qwen3 and $\rho = 0.306$ for MiniLM. However, this increase warrants caution: conditioning on nonzero confusion selects for the dependent variable, which can inflate correlations. We report both estimates for transparency; the all-pairs correlations ($r = 0.112\text{--}0.129$) provide the unbiased baseline, while the nonzero-subset values ($\rho = 0.27\text{--}0.31$) characterize the signal among types the model actually confuses.

-The remaining ${\sim}$98\% of variance in type confusion likely reflects multiple factors: entity and relation frequency in the evaluation corpus, prompt position effects \cite{lost-in-middle-2024}, mention-level ambiguity (e.g., ``Washington'' as person vs.\ location), context complexity, and type definition quality. We frame pairwise SCS as capturing one specific, actionable mechanism---semantic overlap between type labels is directly amenable to schema design and partitioning---rather than the totality of degradation. Although pairwise $r^2$ is modest, the signal compounds at the batch level into accuracy gaps reaching 31.2\,pp under extreme-batch comparison (\S\ref{sec:bcs_controlled}; typical-batch gap ${\approx}\,2\text{--}4$\,pp, \S\ref{sec:practical_magnitude}), demonstrating practical significance for schema optimization.

Critically, 100\% of type confusion errors in RE are intra-batch---the model exclusively confuses types present in the current prompt. The tasks diverge on missed-entity rates: RE rates remain flat (10--16\%), but NER rates are substantially higher (43--65\%) and non-monotonic, suggesting that confusable type sets impair entity detection itself in span-level extraction. lines: \paragraph{Cross-model validation.}

The confusability effect replicates on Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: on FewRel, the BCS gap is $-$27.1\,pp at count${}\,=\,8$ (low-BCS 78.1\% vs.\ high-BCS 51.0\%) and $-$23.9\,pp at count${}\,=\,16$ (75.5\% vs.\ 51.6\%), reaching 77--87\% of Qwen3-32B's $-$31.2\,pp extreme-batch gap. Strikingly, high-BCS accuracy is consistent across tested models (Qwen3-32B and Llama-3.1-8B): both models converge to $\approx$51\% under high confusability (count${}\,=\,8$: 51.0\% vs.\ 51.0\%; count${}\,=\,16$: 51.6\% vs.\ 51.6\%), while cross-model divergence is confined to the low-BCS regime where model capacity matters. This pattern indicates that confusable type sets create a task-inherent difficulty floor consistent across the tested models.
+\paragraph{Prompt sensitivity.}

+The confusability effect is modulated by prompt design. Under the v2 prompt (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_prompt_sensitivity}), the RE extreme-batch gap is attenuated from 31.2\,pp to 7.9\,pp (95\% CI: [$-$5.2, $+$21.5], $n = 5$ batches per level). The effect is attenuated and does not reach significance at $n = 5$. This modulation is specific to the batch-level BCS--accuracy relationship; the underlying pairwise SCS--confusion correlation is embedding-based and therefore prompt-invariant. On NER, v2 actually strengthens the per-type BCS--F1 correlation ($r = +0.58$ vs.\ $+0.50$ under v1), likely because reduced over-prediction yields cleaner confusion signal. Prompt design thus modulates the practical magnitude of the confusability effect, while the underlying type-similarity structure remains a robust predictor of extraction difficulty (see Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_prompt_sensitivity} for full v1/v2 comparison).

lines: \section{Why Naive Decomposition Fails}
\label{sec:sdgd}

-A natural intervention is to partition the schema so confusable types never co-occur. We test this with \textbf{Schema-DAG-Guided Decomposition} (SDGD), which uses greedy graph coloring on the pairwise SCS graph to assign types to low-confusability batches, merging predictions via set union. Every decomposition mode---SDGD (F1\,=\,0.241), random batching (0.320), per-type (0.292)---falls below the single-pass baseline (0.445) on Few-NERD (Table~\ref{tab:sdgd_results}). The bottleneck is \emph{merge amplification}: multiple passes accumulate contradictory predictions at union, destroying precision faster than decomposition helps recall. Confidence-gated merge does not resolve this, as poorly calibrated LLM scores \cite{llm-calibration-survey-2024} discard correct predictions as aggressively as false positives---a structural challenge with direct implications for \citet{llm-pee-2025}. Full experimental details including v1/v2 comparisons are in Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_sdgd}.

+A natural intervention is to partition the schema so confusable types never co-occur. We test this with \textbf{Schema-DAG-Guided Decomposition} (SDGD), which uses greedy graph coloring on the pairwise SCS graph to assign types to low-confusability batches, merging predictions via set union. Every decomposition mode---SDGD (F1\,=\,0.241), random batching (0.320), per-type (0.292)---falls below the single-pass baseline (0.445) on Few-NERD (Table~\ref{tab:sdgd_results}).
+\paragraph{Merge amplification as the bottleneck.}

+The failure mechanism is \emph{merge amplification}: presenting the same text $k$ times with different type subsets causes each pass to independently generate predictions. Single-pass precision is 0.563; after union merge with 8 batches, precision drops to 0.210--0.249 ($-$41--63\%), while recall increases only modestly (0.368 $\to$ 0.314--0.446). The net effect is a precision collapse that overwhelms recall gains (see Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_sdgd}, Table~\ref{tab:sdgd_results} for full breakdown). The fundamental issue is that LLM predictions are not calibrated across passes: a span predicted with high confidence in batch~1 may be contradicted by a different prediction in batch~4, and union merge has no principled way to adjudicate.
+\paragraph{Confidence gating does not resolve the problem.}

+Our v2 merge retains only the highest-confidence prediction per span. This improves precision (sdgd\_zero: 0.210 $\to$ 0.324; random\_batch: 0.249 $\to$ 0.331) but at the cost of disproportionate recall loss (0.314 $\to$ 0.191; 0.446 $\to$ 0.276), yielding lower F1 in both modes. Poorly calibrated LLM confidence scores \cite{llm-calibration-survey-2024} discard correct predictions as aggressively as false positives---a structural challenge with direct implications for any decompose-then-merge pipeline, including \citet{llm-pee-2025}'s event schema partitioning.
